articles.title: Judges must speak
articles.content: A JUDGMENT is a public document, written in the name of the Constitution and delivered in open court. The people may read it, praise it and criticise it, and the academy, bar, press and civil society should do so freely. Criticism is not the enemy of judicial authority; it is its source. A judiciary whose judgments are never read critically will never grow. One voice is largely missing from that conversation: the judge who wrote the judgment. In Pakistan, judges mostly retire into silence. That must change. Retired judges must come out among the people, above all into the law schools, and explain their reasoning, or say, with hindsight: “I think I got that one wrong.” Such candour teaches the profession and builds public trust and confidence in the institution. A sitting judge who knows retirement means facing the public will brush nothing under the carpet. A judgment open to criticism falls into one of three kinds. The first plainly violates the Constitution and the law. The second was legally permissible when given, but its consequences proved damaging. The third is the judgment in which the judge was complicit, bending the law to reach an outcome decided elsewhere. To assess one, read it whole and in context: the moment, the circumstances, the law as it then stood. Then ask whether it was permissible, plainly wrong, or the judge simply listening to power. In Pakistan, judges mostly retire into silence. That must change. In the2023 caseon Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa elections, Justice Jamal Khan Mandokhail and I wanted the high courts to decide first: Lahore had already ordered elections, with appeals pending, and Peshawar was seized of the petitions. Law and practice both counselled that restraint. We read the outcome as four to three, because two colleagues who had already voted to dismiss could not, in our view, be dropped from the count; Justice Athar Minallah, one of them, recorded as much. In hindsight, the mistake, I believe, was the chief justice’s hurried leap in; hearing the matter in appeal, the court could have spoken with one voice. Had we set the count aside and presented a united court, whether that would have produced elections is anyone’s guess. Later, the chief justice’s own bench rejected the four-three objection and fixed May 14 for Punjab polls, yet could not enforce it. The date passed, contempt was never pursued, and the court fell silent. The larger lesson is that a court must stand united, and the chief justice’s strength is the real spine that holds it together. The Supreme Court as it stands today shows how much rests on that spine. In theJustice Qazi Faez Isa case, the court unanimously quashed the reference, the majority for malice in law; I held it malicious in fact as well. The majority directed the FBR to examine the family’s properties and report to the council; three of us held that no direction was needed, the FBR being free to act under the tax law. On review, that view prevailed. No one is above the law, and no one below its protection: a judge’s spouse answers under the tax law, a judge under the Code of Conduct, only in accordance with law. I am often asked whether we saved the wrong man. We saved due process and the independence of the judiciary, and in doing so we saved a man. What people thought of him later was not our concern then. A judgment is not a character certificate. In the Practice and Procedure case, I believed, and still believe, that the court had to become collegial rather than be run by one man. Opening the door was not itself the mistake; so long as the court stood united, no one could have walked through it. What we failed to see was that the court was weak within, and weakness inside invites those outside. And it did: a 2024 ordinance gave the chief justice’s nominee a seat on the bench-forming committee. Had earlier chief justices brought in the collegial model through the full court, that door need never have opened from outside. This is a lesson, not an accusation. Each choice was made in good faith, within the law. In hindsight, wiser choices may have been available, but choosing in the moment is the judicial function, and there the judge must be trusted. Unless a judge was complicit, there is nothing to apologise for, only lessons to share. What must worry us most is complicity. It is not an error of judgment but a surrender of it, and it has hollowed out our courts. A judgment bent to power may be overruled, but the betrayal stays on the record. Error is part of judging. Capitulation is not. And complicity has a way of showing its face, in the promotions, benefits and advantages that later reward it. Today, that trail must be made visible. A word to the critics. Those quick to call out judicial error must be as open-hearted in acknowledging courage. Dissent, refusal of oath and resignation are the building blocks of an independent judiciary. Ask what a judge gained by resigning when a simple yes would have secured everything. Nothing, except the honour of the institution. Criticism that records every failure and never that courage leaves the next generation no one to look up to. So let the conversation begin, and let it be honest. Let judges speak: give the context of their decisions, own their errors without fear and explain their choices without apology. And let complicity be named for what it is. Judicial independence has never been absolute. Sadly, there has always been a chink in the armour, a door left ajar, and someone willing to push it open. No single judgment or judge will close that door. But an honest and open conversation, carried from one generation to the next, can. That will be the real victory: not a court that never errs, but a court with no door through which power can enter. The writer is a professor of practice at SAHSOL, Lums, and currently a distinguished visiting fellow at Yale University.
articles.author: Justice (retd) Syed Mansoor Ali Shah

articles.title: Middle power aspirations
articles.content: AS the global order shifts away from unipolarity toward fragmented multipolarity, middle powers have gained unprecedented strategic weight. In a fragmented multipolar world, middle powers serve as indispensable diplomatic bridges and economic shock absorbers that keep the international system functioning despite great-power paralysis. Middle powers lack hegemonic ambitions, and retain the credibility to mediate active conflicts, build agile issue-specific coalitions, and maintain open trade and supply-chain corridors across rival blocs. Ultimately, these middle powers are preventing total global bifurcation of the international system between Washington and Beijing by stabilising their immediate regions and upholding international rules. However, scholars and policymakers rarely agree on a single checklist for middle power status, largely because different states exert influence through different mechanisms. Some, such as South Korea or Australia, earn the label through thriving, high-tech economies and global trade integration. Others, like Norway or Qatar, leverage niche diplomacy and active mediation to punch above their geographic weight. Still others, such as Türkiye and Pakistan, rely primarily on formidable military capabilities and regional security projection. Scholars generally evaluate middle power status across three core pillars including military capability, diplomatic outreach, and comprehensive national strength. National strength is largely defined by sustainable economic vitality and technological adaptation. Over the past two years, Pakistan has demonstrated a resurgence in the first two arenas, vaulting itself back into global strategic relevance. Yet, because its third and most foundational pillar remains weak, Pakistan’s recognition as an emerging middle power rests on a fragile foundation that cannot endure without a decisive domestic economic pivot. A credible middle power must possess the military capacity to defend its sovereignty and project stabilising influence across its neighbourhood. Between 2025 and 2026, Pakistan highlighted its hard-power credentials through both high-intensity deterrence and institutionaliseddefence partnerships. History shows that hard power and ingenious statecraft cannot substitute for domestic economic strength. During the brief but severefour-day conflictwith India in May 2025, South Asia witnessed its first multi-domain confrontation integrating aerial clashes, drone swarms, and precision missile exchanges. Pakistan’s military response, culminating in Operation Bunyanum Marsoos, demonstrated modern warfare capabilities and aerial superiority. Pakistan’s swift military response compelled a rapid White House-facilitated ceasefire on May 10. By denying a larger neighbour unilateral escalation dominance, Islamabad reinforced its conventional and strategic deterrence. Since May 2025, Pakistan translated its battlefield credibility into a web of security pacts across the Middle East and the Muslim world. In September 2025, Islamabad and Riyadh signed the Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, and in August 2026, Pakistan joined Saudi Arabia and Türkiye to sign the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement. These pacts not only created a formal collective deterrence network but also enhanced Islamabad’s strategic utility in the Gulf. The Badr agreement with Türkiye, Qatar, and Indonesia, has further strengthened Pakistan’s position as a net security provider of Arab Gulf states. Beyond military muscle, middle powers distinguish themselves through niche diplomacy. Following the outbreak of direct US-Israeli military hostilities against Iran in early 2026, traditional Gulf mediators found their channels strained. Adopting a posture of active neutrality, Islamabad stepped in. In March 2026, the US accepted Pakistan’s role as a primary conduit to Tehran, which led to the historic Islamabad peace talks in April 2026 and the subsequent June MoU that temporarily reopened the Strait of Hormuz. Even as the truce faced repeated strain through late 2026, the civil and military leadership of Pakistan continued shuttling proposals between Washington, Tehran, and European capitals. The decision to join Trump’s Gaza peace plan as a founding member also proved Islamabad could exercise diplomatic power beyond its immediate borders. However, despite these military and diplomatic milestones, history demonstrates that hard power and ingenious statecraft cannot substitute for domestic economic strength. In this third pillar, Pakistan exhibits severe structural deficits that undermine its middle power aspirations. Macroeconomic indicators showed surface stabilisation in FY2025-26 with inflation remaining between 7-9 per cent and GDP growth edging up to 3.7pc. However, the underlying growth model remains weak. For instance, investment hovers near 15pc of GDP, far below the 20-plus per cent threshold required to sustain the 6pc growth rates needed to absorb a booming youth population. Deindustrialisation and high energy costs continue to stifle export competitiveness. Foreign investors are largely concerned with the security situation in Balochistan and KP. Unrest in AJK has further marred prospects of foreign direct investment. The privatisation process is critically slow, while political consensus is absent over reforms for new provinces. With a low tax-to-GDP ratio and heavy external debt servicing, state solvency still relies heavily on remittances, multilateral bailouts, bilateral rollovers (such as a $3 billion Saudi cash deposit in April 2026) rather than productive capital formation. Hence, Pakistan today represents a textbook case of an asymmetric emerging middle power. Its disciplined military and seasoned diplomatic corps have successfully leveraged regional crises to earn Islamabad a seat at high-stakes global tables. However, geopolitical leverage built on security crises and external rent is inherently transactional. When regional wars subside or great-power priorities shift, Islamabad — lacking economic autonomy and technological innovation — will risk losing its strategic relevance. Therefore, to cement its status as a genuine middle power, Pakistan must execute an urgent domestic pivot. This requires dismantling elite economic capture, broadening the tax base, overhauling education to build a tech-literate workforce, and enhancing an export-driven industrial base. Until Islamabad matches its battlefield deterrence and diplomatic agility with sustainable economic sovereignty, its middle power status will remain an aspiration suspended over a precarious fault line. The writer is a strategic analyst of international security. The views expressed are his own.
articles.author: Khurram Abbas

articles.title: Good girl rules
articles.content: I STARTED watching Dar-i-Nijaat because my friend Sahar has been writing about the drama, and we have agreed on most things for longer than either of us would like to admit. Not this time. Sahar sees a story about compassion. I see a story about conditions. It may be the first time we have so firmly disagreed. Thankfully, we have been friends far longer than Abu Bakar has been on air. He won’t come between us. Because that is who everyone is talking about. Abu Bakar, the patient husband half of South Asia seems to have fallen for. I expected to write about him. Instead, I am thinking about Zaryab, who I spent most of the show frustrated with. I am still not sure what the story is asking of her. But I know exactly what everyone else is. They want gratitude. A woman with a past has been taken in by a good man, and she should know how lucky she is. They want shame. Her relationship with Zamil before marriage, which writer Umera Ahmed confirmed when a fan asked her online, is treated as a stain that must be visible before it can be washed away. And they want a change of heart, ideally a dramatic one, so that by the end, the girl who once put a man ahead of Harvard can be returned to us as a “good wife.” Zaryab, to her credit or her cost, does not initially cooperate. She is sharp, self-absorbed and frequently unbearable. I notice that much of the irritation around her comes with a rulebook attached. A lot of us are not just judging a character. We are checking whether she has behaved correctly as a woman who has fallen. We seem to prefer the penitent over the feminist. That rulebook is old. Pakistani television has always sorted its women. The good girl is patient, modest and forgiving, and she is rewarded with love, a home and, eventually, respect. The bad girl wants things. She is ambitious, impatient or careless with her reputation, and she is punished, cast out or redeemed only when someone better decides she is worth saving. Salvation is not something Zaryab earns; it is something Abu Bakar extends. The story decides she is worth saving because a good man decides she is. The easy answer is the writer. Umera Ahmed has built a career on stories of faith and redemption, and I guess she does it well — this is the first play of hers I’m watching. I got sucked in, despite myself. But a writer does not work alone. There are producers who choose which stories get made, channels that decide what fills prime time, and actors who shape how a character lands. The company that produced the drama was co-founded by ARY’s chief executive and by Sheheryar Munawar, who plays Abu Bakar. The man at the centre of the story also helped bring it to the screen. And then there is us. The drama’s makers say it has drawn more than 1.7 billion views across social media. We fill the comment sections with verdicts. She doesn’t deserve him. She should be grateful. Wait until she learns her lesson. Every season, the industry learns what we reward, and gives us more of it. It wasn’t always like this. There are so many great roles to cite about prickly, ambitious and unapologetic women who wanted more than the life they were born into. These women made mistakes. Nobody asked them to be grateful for their own lives. I haven’t watched every drama, and I know there are writers still giving us women with spines. But a single drama is a story. A shift is a signal. When the women who draw the biggest audiences are the ones who are forgiven rather than the ones who fight, it tells us something about what we have come to expect of women, on screen and off. We seem to prefer the penitent over the feminist. We live in a country where women are still killed in the name of honour, where a woman’s past can be treated as a crime and her husband as her judge. Stories do not cause that. But stories that teach us a woman with a past is damaged goods, salvageable only through a forgiving man, make it easier to believe. They tell girls what they owe. They tell boys what they are owed. I would like, just once, to watch a Zaryab who is not asked for gratitude, shame or a change of heart. Who makes mistakes, lives with them and grows on her own terms. Who might even go back to Harvard, not as a reward for good behaviour, but because she wants to. Would we watch that? Or would we fill the comments asking when she plans to say sorry? The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: Contested frontier
articles.content: IN a new movie starring Salman Khan, Bollywood has smartly invested in a tale that can reap financial benefits by inflaming the emotions of Indians still traumatised by 1962. But behind the Galwan incident of 2020 lies a tale that is far more fascinating than the movie itself: the riveting story of the Sino-Indian border. But let us rewind first to the 19th century, when Russia and Britain were fearful that their nemesis was advancing towards an area stretching from present-day Afghanistan to Tibet. Kashmir had come under British control in 1846, but it was not clear where the boundary lay between Ladakh and Tibet. A map drawn by W.H. Johnson suggested that Aksai Chin lay within Kashmir, but later, in 1899, the British proposed a different boundary to China, which showed that a big chunk of Aksai Chin belonged to the latter. In short, there was neither delimitation (verbal or written agreement) nor demarcation (marking the line on the ground) of the border between China and British India in the Western Sector. Enter the Eastern Sector. Here, again, no boundary existed between China and British India, but the latter did adhere to the so-called Inner and Outer Lines. However, in 1913-14, the momentous Simla Conference was held, attended by representatives of British India, China and Tibet. Britain proposed dividing Tibet into Inner and Outer zones. A weak China asked its envoy to leave and thus, in a moment of great wisdom, saved itself from calamity. However, Tibet, which was claimed by China on the basis of both international treaties and custom, and Britain did sign an agreement, a secret part of which specified the McMahon Line (MML) as the border between India and Chinese Tibet. The border was thus delimited but not demarcated, and was not agreed upon by China. The line was drawn by a marker whose width on the map would cover many mountain crests. Move forward to 1959. By now, India had gained independence, China had moved from weakness to strength and re-established control over Tibet, the Dalai Lama had fled Tibet to seek refuge in India, Nehru was firmly in command of India, and had extended India’s control up to the MML, but there was still no boundary in the Western Sector. And China had been suggesting to India that they stabilise the border, to no avail. Nehru completely misread what China wanted. Nehru was a great leader with two minor blemishes: he ruined India’s economy and he ruined India’s relations with China. He now made three pivotal blunders which would have a long-term impact. First, he completely misread what China wanted. China wanted to settle the border with India around the MML, with one proviso: negotiations on the MML should be held afresh. Why? Remember, the MML was agreed upon by the British and the Tibetans. If China agreed to the MML, it would have to admit that Tibet in 1913-14 was independent. Second, Aksai Chin, some 15,000sq miles of barren land, was of no use to India but was vital to China because of the presence of a road which connects Tibet with Xinjiang. China would have ceded the North-East Frontier Agency’s (NEFA) 40,000sq miles to India but would never have accepted Indian control over Aksai Chin. Third, in one of the most self-harming moves, Nehru initiated his infamous ‘Forward Policy.’ Remember, the borders in both sectors were not demarcated. And we are talking about some of the highest, roughest landscapes here. Nehru ordered Indian troops to move forward and start occupying the spaces in between the Chinese outposts, and even fire upon the Chinese to vacate their posts. The Indian generals warned Nehru against this madness, but to no avail. A senior Chinese diplomat told me, “they started cutting up our soldiers to pieces and we did not move a muscle.” On Oct 20, 1962, the Chinese, fed up, attacked across both sectors. The Indian 7 Brigade dissolved into thin air. The war was over as soon as it began. The Chinese occupied NEFA, and, in one of the most astonishing moments in world history, declared that they would unilaterally withdraw. The war left Nehru’s reputation in tatters. It ‘gifted’ Kashmir to Pakistan on a silver platter, and led India into making a U-turn and accepting the West’s military aid. The war also sowed the seeds of an en-mity which was many times more pronounced in an India where the population was never told the truth than in China, where much saner minds had been in command. In 2026, when Salman Khan’s movie on the Galwan incident of 2020 is released to an emotional population, the latter will not be told that it was Nehru’s hubris, intransigence and folly which had led to this state of affairs. History can be more fascinating than Bollywood movies. The writer has a First-class degree in history from Oxford and has worked in China as a diplomat.
articles.author: Aamir Khan

articles.title: Muddled hierarchy
articles.content: THE Federal Constitutional Court marked its first anniversary on Friday with a commemorative stamp. Speaking on the occasion, its chief justice remarked on how fleeting the year had been. Litigants, lawyers and the judges of the Supreme Court might have described it differently. A year after the 27th Amendment rewrote the structure of the country’s judiciary, one of the most basic questions raised by the new order remains unanswered: which court, the FCC or the SC, has the final word? This was, perhaps, bound to happen. Critics had foreseen problems in the short and hurried route the government took from the 26th to the27th Amendment. In October 2024, the26th Amendmentcarved constitutional benches out of the SC, with their members chosen by a reconstituted Judicial Commission in which judges no longer held a majority. Critics warned then that the independence of the judiciary was at stake. Barely a year later, and in evident haste, the 27th Amendment turned those benches into an entirely separate court. Two of the SC’s senior-most judgesresignedin protest the day it became law. Thousands of cases were soon transferred to the FCC, and the SC was stripped of its constitutional jurisdiction. What has followed has seemed less a division of labour than a contest for primacy. Last December, the FCCheldthat its rulings bind all courts, including the SC, but that the latter’s do not bind the FCC. In May, Chief Justice Yahya Afridi pushed back, ruling that the two are coordinate courts, neither an appellate forum over the other. Last month, the FCC rebuked an SC bench for revisiting a matter the FCC considered settled, raising concerns over judicial discipline. The sparring shows no sign of stopping. The text of the amendment arguably favours the FCC, while the SC relies on the overall constitutional scheme to assert its position. That both positions can be argued is precisely the problem. Two hasty amendments have created an ambiguity that leaves the two courts defining their relationship through pointed observations in their judgments. The costs are borne by litigants, whose cases risk being shuttled between forums. The FCC, meanwhile, has worked with seven judges against a sanctioned strength of 13. And its order barring the Peshawar High Court from hearing petitions on emergency and governor’s rule in KP has pushed citizens away from a court closer to home. Since parliament created this ambiguity, it must now resolve it. The jurisdiction of the two courts and a mechanism for settling disputes between them should be spelt out in law, not left to judges to fight over. Lastly, the judiciary’s structure is not its only problem. As long as its independence remains in doubt, it will struggle to win public confidence.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Growing crisis
articles.content: AN emergency can be judged by the speed with which it draws an effective response. The National Population Council’s executive committee has declared rapid population growth a national emergency. But Pakistan has been warned about this crisis for decades, with little to show for it. People still struggle to obtain reproductive healthcare, clinics run short of contraceptives, and millions of couples lack the information and services needed to plan families. The 2023 census recorded an annual population growth rate of 2.55pc, placing further pressure on schools, hospitals, housing, jobs and water supplies. The state cannot keep announcing plans while failing to provide basic services. One key decision taken at the meeting was to improve the tracking of contraceptive supplies. But collecting data is only the first step. Provinces must ensure that clinics are adequately equipped, healthcare workers are trained and family planning services reach remote and neglected communities. Religious scholars can also help address misconceptions about birth spacing, particularly by explaining its benefits for mothers and children. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal has raised another important issue: the National Finance Commission formula, which gives population an 82pc weight in the distribution of provincial resources. His concern that the formula may reward population growth deserves attention. However, simply giving provinces more money for reducing birth rates could create fresh problems. Provinces with larger, poorer populations already face greater demands for schools, hospitals and other services. Cutting their share would only make these problems worse. Instead, the government should consider rewarding provinces that improve access to family planning, girls’ education and maternal healthcare, while ensuring that funding reflects their actual needs. Above all, the authorities must recognise that population planning is about helping people make informed choices, not merely bringing down numbers. Calling population growth a national emergency is easy. Ensuring that the response reaches the people who need it is the real challenge.
articles.author: Editorial
